explanation: Adding -b to netstat shows the name of the executable that created each connection or listening port, and it works only from an elevated prompt. The -a switch adds listening ports to the list without naming the programs, -n shows addresses and ports as numbers instead of names, and -r prints the routing table.

question: A technician turns on BitLocker for the system drive of a desktop that has no TPM, after enabling the Group Policy setting that allows this. Which protector can unlock the drive at each startup?
options: A TPM and a startup PIN
A smart card and its PIN
explanation: Without a TPM, BitLocker can unlock the system drive at startup only with a startup key on a USB flash drive or with a startup password, once Group Policy allows BitLocker without a compatible TPM. A TPM with a PIN needs the chip this desktop lacks, a smart card can unlock data drives but not the system drive, and a Windows Hello fingerprint signs a user in to Windows only after the drive has been unlocked.

question: A PC with 16 GB of RAM warns that it is low on memory although only two applications are open. Task Manager shows one application's memory use climbing steadily until it is closed. What should the technician do to fix the cause?
options: Increase the size of the paging file
Install an update for the program
Install additional RAM in the computer
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic on restart
explanation: Memory use that keeps climbing in one application until it is closed is a memory leak, a bug that an update to that application fixes, while more memory or paging space only delays the warning. A larger paging file helps when the paging file is too small for normal work, more RAM helps when the usual workload needs more memory, and Windows Memory Diagnostic tests for faulty RAM behind stop errors.

question: During a building-wide blackout, a file server keeps running on stored power for several minutes and then shuts itself down cleanly. Which device made this possible?
explanation: An uninterruptible power supply runs equipment from its battery the moment utility power fails, which gives a server time to shut down cleanly. A surge suppressor absorbs voltage spikes but stores no energy, a power distribution unit spreads power across the outlets in a rack, and an automatic transfer switch moves the load to another source, such as a generator, without storing any power itself.

question: A hospital must destroy a batch of retired hard disks that hold patient records. It can do the work itself with its own staff, or send the disks to a destruction vendor. Which advantage does doing the work itself have?
options: Freeing its staff for other work
Recycling the remains under e-waste rules
Keeping the drives in its custody
explanation: Destroying drives in-house keeps them in the organization's own custody until they are destroyed, so no outsider handles or transports media that still holds data. Using a destruction vendor is what brings a certificate of destruction, recycling of the remains under environmental rules and staff time freed for other work.

question: After typing her password, a user enters a six-digit code that her phone generates every 30 seconds. The code works even when the phone has no signal. Which MFA method is she using?
explanation: An authenticator application on a phone calculates a time-based one-time code from a shared secret and the clock, so it needs no signal and changes every 30 seconds. A hardware token also generates codes offline but is a separate key fob rather than the phone, and a text message code or an automated voice call depends on the phone network to deliver the code.

question: A Windows 11 PC keeps showing alerts in the corner of the screen that say a virus was found and urge the user to renew protection. Each alert names a website as its sender, and a full malware scan is clean. Which action will stop the alerts?
options: Turn off the notifications that Windows Security sends
Revoke that site's permission to send notifications
Run a full scan of the PC with Microsoft Defender Offline
Block pop-ups from that site in the browser's settings
explanation: Scam sites trick users into allowing notifications and then push fake virus alerts that look like Windows messages but name the site as the sender, so revoking that site's notification permission in the browser stops them. Blocking pop-ups does not affect notifications, the alerts do not come from Windows Security, and an offline scan hunts for hidden malware, which a clean full scan and a website sender already point away from.

question: A training company sells video courses and protects each file with digital rights management. What does that protection mainly do?
options: Proves the videos came from the real publisher
Limits how buyers copy or share the videos
Stops staff from leaking the videos outside
Compresses the videos so they stream faster
explanation: Digital rights management controls what buyers can do with content they have paid for, such as limiting copying, sharing or the number of devices that can play it. Proving where a file came from is the job of a digital signature, stopping staff from leaking data is the job of data loss prevention, and compression shrinks files without controlling how they are used.

question: A user installs what looks like a well-known authenticator app from the official app store. The icon and name match, but the publisher is unfamiliar and the app asks for access to text messages and contacts. Which security concern does this show?
explanation: Application spoofing means a fake app that copies the name and icon of a real one to fool users, and an unfamiliar publisher asking for text messages and contacts is a typical sign. An unofficial store is ruled out because the app came from the official store, root access describes a phone whose built-in restrictions have been removed, and developer mode is a settings menu meant for testing apps.

question: An employee is leaving, and a replacement starts next week. The company's cloud productivity suite is licensed per user, and the company has exactly as many licenses as staff. Once the departing employee's data has been handled under company policy, what should the technician do with their license?
options: Buy an additional license and assign it to the new hire
Rename the departed user's account and give it to the new hire
Block sign-in and keep the license on the old account
Unassign the license and reassign it to the new hire
explanation: Per-user subscription licenses belong to the company and are assigned to accounts, so removing the license from the departed user's account frees it for the replacement and no seat is paid for unused. Buying another license wastes money, a blocked account that keeps its license still holds the seat, and handing over the old account mixes two people's activity under one identity.

question: A retailer allows planned changes only on Sundays from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m., and blocks all non-emergency changes from mid-November to early January. What are these two controls?
options: A maintenance window and a change freeze
A rollback plan and a backup plan
explanation: A maintenance window is a set, low-impact time when approved changes may be made, and a change freeze blocks non-emergency changes during critical business periods such as holiday sales. Rollback and backup plans cover recovery from a failed change, sandbox testing and peer review check a change before it goes live, and end-user acceptance and risk analysis evaluate it.

question: A technician suspects that someone has been trying to guess a user's password. Logon auditing is turned on. In Event Viewer, which Windows log should the technician filter for failed sign-in attempts?
explanation: The Security log in Event Viewer holds audit records, such as the failed sign-in attempts (event ID 4625) that Windows writes when logon auditing is turned on. The System log holds events from Windows components such as drivers and services, the Application log holds events written by programs, including their crashes, and the Setup log records installation and update activity.

question: A user on hotel Wi-Fi wants the browser's lookups of website names to be encrypted so that the hotel's network cannot read or alter them. Which browser setting should the user turn on?
explanation: Secure DNS sends the browser's name lookups to a resolver over an encrypted connection (DNS over HTTPS), so the local network cannot read or tamper with them. Private browsing only discards history and cookies when the window closes, safe browsing checks addresses against a list of dangerous sites, and autofill enters saved form data.

question: A company wants each visitor's photo ID checked at the front desk and each entry recorded, with someone on hand to challenge anyone who refuses. Which physical control provides this?
explanation: Security guards are people who can check identification, record visitors and use judgment to challenge or turn away anyone who does not comply. Badge readers check a credential automatically but cannot question a visitor, turnstiles admit one person at a time once access is granted, and motion sensors detect movement in a space after hours.

question: A review finds that anyone at a workstation's sign-in screen could try passwords for its local accounts without limit. Which setting stops this kind of guessing after a few wrong passwords?
explanation: An account lockout threshold locks an account after a set number of failed sign-ins, which turns an unlimited guessing attack into a few attempts. A minimum password length makes passwords harder to guess but allows unlimited tries, a maximum password age forces regular changes, and password history stops users from reusing recent passwords.

question: A school wants its students' accounts on the library workstations to work only during school hours, so that nobody can sign in with them at night or on weekends. Which account setting does this?
explanation: A login time restriction sets the days and hours when an account may sign in and refuses sign-ins at any other time. An account expiration date stops an account from working after a chosen day, a lockout threshold locks an account after a set number of wrong passwords, and a screen lock timeout locks a session that has been left idle.

question: A network team wants each command that an administrator enters on its switches and routers to be authorized separately and logged. Which protocol should the devices use to reach the AAA server?
explanation: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting, so a server can approve or refuse each command an administrator types and log it, which makes it the usual choice for managing network devices. RADIUS combines authentication with authorization and is built for network access such as Wi-Fi and VPNs, Kerberos issues tickets for domain services, and Diameter is the AAA protocol of mobile carrier networks.

question: A laptop runs Windows 11 Home. The user's office PC, which no one else uses, runs Windows 11 Pro, has Remote Desktop turned on and can be reached over the VPN. What happens when the user starts Remote Desktop Connection on the laptop and connects to it?
options: The laptop asks for Remote Desktop to be enabled
The session opens after the user signs in
The office PC asks its user to accept
The laptop says that Home cannot run the client
explanation: Windows 11 Home includes the Remote Desktop Connection client, so it can connect to a computer that hosts sessions, such as one running Pro, and the session opens once the user signs in. Only Pro and higher editions can host sessions, which is why Remote Desktop is turned on at the office PC and not at the laptop, and a prompt to accept appears with Quick Assist, or when a different user is signed in at the host.

question: Before a change to the accounting application is closed, staff from the accounting team work through their daily tasks in the new version and sign to say that it meets their needs. Which step of the change process is this?
explanation: End-user acceptance is the step in which the people who use a system confirm that the change works for their real tasks before the change is closed. Change board approval comes before any work starts, peer review has another technician check the plan or the work, and a post-implementation review is the IT team's own look back at how the change went.

question: Each night a backup folder on a file server must become an exact copy of a department share: new and changed files are copied, and files deleted from the share are removed from the backup. Which command does this?
explanation: The robocopy /mir switch mirrors a folder tree: it copies new and changed files and deletes from the destination anything that no longer exists in the source. With /move, robocopy deletes files from the source after copying them, xcopy /e /d copies the tree and only newer files but deletes nothing, and xcopy /e /h adds hidden and system files to a full copy.

question: On her first day, an employee signs a document agreeing not to install unapproved software, visit gambling sites or run a side business from her work email. What is this document?
explanation: An acceptable use policy sets out what employees may and may not do with company computers, networks, email and internet access, and staff usually sign it when they join. A nondisclosure agreement covers keeping information confidential, a new-user setup checklist guides IT through creating the account, and a standard operating procedure explains how to carry out a task.

question: A field technician's map app places her at the correct position, but the arrow for the direction she is facing points the wrong way, even in an open field. What should she do first?
explanation: The arrow that shows which way a phone is facing comes from its magnetometer, the compass sensor, so a correct position with a wrong heading calls for calibrating the compass, usually by moving the phone in a figure-eight pattern. High-accuracy location uses Wi-Fi and cell towers to improve the position rather than the heading, clearing the map app's cache fixes display glitches, and the SIM card has nothing to do with the compass.

question: A PC shows unwanted pop-up notifications advertising system cleanup deals, from an app the user does not remember installing. Which step BEST addresses both the symptom and its cause?
options: Turn off notifications for the app in the Settings app
Block the app's outbound connections in the firewall
Uninstall the app from the Apps section of the Settings app
Revoke the notification permissions held by each browser
explanation: Notifications from an app the user never chose are a sign of adware or another potentially unwanted program, so uninstalling the app removes their source, and a follow-up anti-malware scan catches anything installed with it. Turning off the app's notifications only hides them, browser permissions control notifications from websites rather than from installed apps, and a firewall rule leaves the program on the PC.

question: A technician is deciding between a clean install and an in-place upgrade of Windows 11 on a user's PC. Which situation calls for the clean install?
options: The user needs apps and files left in place
The PC needs the latest Windows feature update
A rootkit has infected the current system
A few system files have become damaged
explanation: A clean install erases the old system and starts again from trusted media, so it is the choice when malware such as a rootkit means the current installation can no longer be trusted. An in-place upgrade is the choice when apps and files must stay or a feature update is due, and a repair install or System File Checker fixes a few damaged system files.

question: A browser's task manager shows an extension called PDF Helper, added last week from a pop-up ad, using 80 percent of the CPU at all times with steady memory use, even when no PDF files are open. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: Hardware acceleration turned off in the browser
A keylogger recording what the user types
A memory leak in the extension's code
A cryptocurrency miner inside the extension
explanation: An extension that keeps the processor busy while it has no work to do is doing hidden work, and one added from a pop-up ad is most likely mining cryptocurrency, so it should be removed and the PC scanned. A memory leak would show as growing memory use, a keylogger needs very little processor time, and turning off hardware acceleration moves page rendering onto the processor without singling out one extension.

question: A Windows 11 Pro PC can ping the company's domain controller, 10.1.1.53, by IP address, but joining the domain fails with a message that no domain controller could be contacted. Which setting should the technician correct?
explanation: Active Directory clients find domain controllers through records in the domain's DNS zone, so a PC that points to a public or router DNS server cannot locate one even when it can reach it by IP address. Because the controller answers a ping, the gateway and subnet mask are not blocking traffic to it, and the computer name only sets what the PC will be called in the domain.

question: A small office backs up its file server each night to one external drive, and each run replaces the previous night's copy. Which loss would leave the office with no good copy to restore?
options: A database damaged by a crash during the workday
A file corrupted weeks before anyone noticed
A server drive that fails after the nightly run
A folder deleted by mistake earlier the same day
explanation: A scheme that keeps one generation can return data only to its state at the last run, so damage that goes unnoticed past the next run is copied over the last good version. A failed drive, a folder deleted earlier that day and a database damaged in a crash can all be restored from the previous night's copy, while keeping older generations, as a grandfather-father-son rotation does, would have saved the corrupted file.

question: A user joins videoconferences in a web browser. Others can see the user's video but cannot hear them, and the browser shows a crossed-out microphone icon in the address bar. What should the technician check FIRST?
options: The playback device selected in the Windows sound settings
The camera permission for the site in the browser settings
The microphone driver listed in Windows Device Manager
The microphone permission for the site in the browser
explanation: A crossed-out microphone icon in the address bar means the browser has blocked the site from using the microphone, so the fix starts with allowing it in the site's permissions, then confirming that Windows lets the browser use the microphone. The camera permission already works because others see the video, the playback device affects what the user hears, and a driver fault would leave the browser with no microphone to offer rather than a blocked one.

question: After a technician adjusts an office wireless router, the network no longer appears in the list of available networks on new laptops, though users who type its name by hand can still connect. Which change did the technician make?
explanation: Disabling SSID broadcast leaves the network name out of the router's beacon frames, so the network drops out of the list of available networks and users must enter the name by hand. A new channel or a new SSID would still be listed, and MAC address filtering refuses unlisted devices while leaving the network visible. Hiding the name is a weak control, because the name still travels in other wireless frames.

question: A user installs a 32-bit accounting program on a Windows 11 PC, and it runs normally. Which Windows component makes this possible?
explanation: WOW64 (Windows 32-bit on Windows 64-bit) is the subsystem that runs 32-bit programs on 64-bit Windows, and every edition of Windows 11 is 64-bit. Such programs install to the Program Files (x86) folder by default. WSL 2 runs Linux programs, Hyper-V runs whole operating systems in virtual machines, and Windows Sandbox runs programs in a temporary, isolated desktop.

question: A company wants employees to use generative AI with internal documents, without that data leaving the company's control or being used to train the provider's models. Which option fits BEST?
options: An AI model that the company hosts on its own servers
A public AI service reached over the company's VPN
An AI browser extension that IT has approved and installed
A free chatbot account with its training setting turned off
explanation: Private AI runs in an environment the organization controls or contracts for, such as a self-hosted model or an enterprise service with data protection terms, so prompts and documents stay inside its boundary and are not used for training. Turning off training on a free chatbot account still sends the documents to the provider, an approved extension still passes them to its developer's service, and a VPN protects traffic in transit without changing what the AI provider does with it.

question: Antivirus software running inside Windows reports a clean PC, but a scan started from bootable media finds a modified system driver that was hiding a process and its files from Task Manager and File Explorer. Which type of malware is this?
explanation: A rootkit hides itself by modifying core parts of the operating system, such as drivers, so that tools running inside Windows cannot see it, and a scan from bootable media can find it because the rootkit is not running. A boot sector virus infects the boot code on the disk rather than a driver, fileless malware leaves no modified file to find, and a keylogger records keystrokes rather than hiding other software.

question: Before examining a seized drive, an investigator makes a bit-for-bit image of it and records a hash of both the drive and the image. Why is the hash recorded?
options: To keep the image unreadable without a key
To prove the image matches the original
To record who has handled the evidence
To shrink the image so it takes less space
explanation: A hash works as a fingerprint of the data, so matching hashes for the drive and its image prove that the copy is exact and that neither has changed since, which keeps the evidence usable. The record of who handled the evidence is the chain of custody, keeping data unreadable without a key is encryption, and shrinking an image is compression, none of which a hash does.

question: A technician whose own firm requires suits is booked for a visit to a client that asks all visitors to wear slacks and a collared shirt, without a jacket or tie. What should the technician wear?
explanation: A technician should dress to the client's standard, and slacks with a collared shirt but no jacket or tie is business casual attire. Formal business attire, a suit and tie, is right for a client that expects it but goes against this request, casual work clothes such as jeans fit a relaxed workplace, and protective work clothing is for a factory floor or a building site.

question: Responders to a data breach are told not to shut down the affected server until evidence has been collected from it. What would a shutdown destroy?
explanation: Anything held only in RAM, such as running processes, open network connections and encryption keys, disappears when power is removed, so it must be captured before any shutdown. Event logs, scheduled tasks, user files, installed programs and firmware settings are kept on disk or in nonvolatile memory, so they survive a shutdown and can be examined afterward.
